reading.title: Reading Clues from an Ancient Village
reading.purpose: Discover how archaeologists separate solid evidence from careful guesses.
paras: When archaeologists uncover the stone walls of a thousand-year-old village, they rarely find written signs explaining every room. Instead, they gather pottery shards, charred seeds, and animal bones, then weigh how certain each conclusion really is. Good researchers never simply assume a fact without checking the ground first, because an unchecked guess can mislead an entire dig.

Suppose a team finds three large clay ovens beside a wide courtyard. They might surmise from those limited clues that neighbors baked bread together in a shared space. That explanation sounds plausible, reasonable and believable based on how similar towns worked. Still, until they test the ash and map nearby doorways, the team treats its report as tentative, open to change whenever new evidence turns up.

Sometimes a lab test comes back inconclusive, failing to point to one clear answer. A trace of pollen on a stone tool could mean the tool cut grain, or wind might have blown pollen onto it centuries later. Rather than treat a hunch as proof, scientists label an unproven guess as conjecture. They may also build a hypothetical model—an imagined test scenario—to check what kind of wear marks different crops would leave on flint.

Fieldwork also brings unforeseen surprises, unexpected discoveries that arrive without warning. A sudden rainstorm might wash away topsoil and reveal a hidden canal no one knew existed. Researchers cannot presume that an ancient community stayed the same for centuries; they ask which explanation is most probable given all the layers uncovered so far. Honest science is not embarrassed by uncertainty—it measures it carefully.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "tentative" most nearly means
choices: proven beyond doubt by three separate lab reports
not final yet and open to change with new evidence
buried under thick layers of clay and burned ash
impossible to test without written village records
qs.why: Paragraph 2 explains tentative directly as "open to change whenever new evidence turns up."

qs.q: Which sentence shows why pollen on a stone tool might not prove what the tool was used for?
choices: Sometimes a lab test comes back inconclusive, failing to point to one clear answer.
A trace of pollen on a stone tool could mean the tool cut grain, or wind might have blown pollen onto it centuries later.
Rather than treat a hunch as proof, scientists label an unproven guess as conjecture.
Fieldwork also brings unforeseen surprises, unexpected discoveries that arrive without warning.
qs.why: This sentence gives two competing explanations for the pollen, showing why the trace alone is not definitive proof.

ev.text: A trace of pollen on a stone tool could mean the tool cut grain, or wind might have blown pollen onto it centuries later.

qs.q: Why does the author say honest science is not embarrassed by uncertainty?
choices: Naming what is only probable or unproven keeps researchers open to better evidence.
Archaeologists prefer guessing from pottery shards rather than running careful lab tests.
Rainstorms usually wash away every important canal before a dig can even begin.
Ancient villages never left behind enough bones or seeds to learn anything real.
qs.why: Throughout the text, labeling conclusions as tentative or conjecture helps scientists revise ideas when new clues appear.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Shared clay ovens prove that every ancient village baked bread in a central courtyard.
Archaeologists carefully distinguish between solid proof, reasonable guesses, and open questions.
Pollen tests are rarely worth running because wind blows dust across every stone tool.
Sudden rainstorms are more helpful to historians than careful digging or lab models.
qs.why: The reading explains how archaeologists weigh degrees of certainty using tentative claims, models, and new evidence.

clues.text: failing to point to one clear answer
unexpected discoveries that arrive without warning
